dualgoal.noteBase: Base phase – the ideal time to lose weight: a moderate deficit with plenty of easy volume.

dualgoal.noteTaper: Taper – refuel now instead of losing weight: eat well so you’re fit for race day.
dualgoal.stimulusEnough: Your training gives you enough stimulus for real progress.
dualgoal.stimulusLow: Not much challenging stimulus lately – rest days alone won’t bring you closer to your goal. Plan key sessions again (stimulus + recovery = progress).

fullBody.title: Full body
fullBody.desc: Full body, 3 rounds (bodyweight or with dumbbells/kettlebell): Squats 12× · Push-ups 8–12× (on your knees if needed) · Lunges 10×/leg · Shoulder press 12× · Plank 30–45 s. Clean technique before weight, 60–90 s rest between rounds.

legs.title: Legs & glutes
legs.desc: Leg strength for a stable running form, 3 rounds: Squats 15× · Romanian deadlift (dumbbell/kettlebell or single-leg) 10× · Step-ups onto a bench/step 10×/leg · Calf raises 20× (half of them with bent knees) · Glute bridge 15×. With weights a few reps fewer, 60–90 s rest.

core.title: Trunk & core
core.desc: Core stability for an upright running posture, 3 rounds: Plank 40 s · Side plank 30 s/side · Dead bug 10×/side · Bird dog 10×/side (on all fours, extend opposite arm and leg without arching your back) · Russian twists 20×. Slow and controlled, keep your body tension on purpose.

legsPush.title: Strength – Legs & pushing
legsPush.desc: 3–4 rounds: Squats or leg press 8–10× · Weighted lunges 10×/leg · Sled push or wall sit 45 s · Push-ups 10× · Plank 40 s. Heavy but clean – 90 s rest between rounds.

pullGrip.title: Strength – Pulling & grip
pullGrip.desc: 3–4 rounds: Romanian deadlift 8× · Bent-over row 10× · Farmer’s carry 2×30 m heavy · Lat pulldown or negative pull-ups 8× · Dead bug 10×/side. Grip strength pays off in the Farmer’s carry and the sled pull.

fullBody.title: Strength – Full body & wall balls
fullBody.desc: 3 rounds: Front squat or thrusters 10× · Wall balls 15× · Kettlebell swings 15× · Sandbag or dumbbell lunges 20 m · Burpees 8×. Brisk, but with clean technique.

short.one: For {race} at the “{level}” level we recommend at least {minWeeks} weeks of preparation – you have {count} week until the race. You could choose a later race, a shorter distance or the goal “finish healthy” without a target time. Either way, the plan only builds volume gently.

hyroxRun.title: Hyrox running {n}×1 km
hyroxRun.desc: {warm} warm-up, then {n}×1 km brisk (Z4, around threshold pace) with {pause} rest after each – just like between the stations in the race: catch your breath after the kilometre, then find your pace again. {cool} cool-down.

baseRun.title: Easy run with strides
baseRun.desc: Easy run in Z2 (conversational pace). In the last 1–2 km, add 5–6 strides of ~80–100 m: jog in easily, accelerate over ~20 m to about 90 % (fast, but not a sprint), then let it roll out. Walk or jog easily for 60–90 s in between. Heart rate doesn’t matter here – it’s about speed and clean technique.

threshold.title: Threshold run {n}×{min} min
threshold.marathonDesc: Marathon-specific: {warm} easy warm-up. Then {n}×12 min at threshold (Z4, “comfortably hard”) with 3 min easy jogging after each – long, steady efforts instead of short peaks. {cool} cool-down. In a marathon, endurance at the upper end of your pace range is what counts.
threshold.desc6: {warm} easy warm-up (Z2). Then {n}×6 min at threshold (Z4, “comfortably hard” – you could still speak short sentences) at your target pace, with 2 min very easy jogging in between. Finish with {cool} cool-down. Stay even – don’t overdo the first interval.
threshold.desc8: {warm} easy, {n}×8 min at threshold (Z4) with 2 min jog recovery, {cool} cool-down. Keeps your speed endurance without draining your legs the way VO₂max intervals do.

fartlek.title: Fartlek {n}×(1 min fast / 1 min easy)
fartlek.desc: {warm} easy warm-up. Then {n}×1 min brisk (Z4, “comfortably hard”), with 1 min of very easy running in between (don’t stop) – a flowing fartlek. Hold the pace without sprinting. {cool} cool-down.

marathonPace.title: Marathon race pace {n}×4 km
marathonPace.desc: Race-pace specific: {warm} easy, then {n}×4 km at your target marathon pace (controlled but brisk) with 3 min easy jogging after each. {cool} cool-down. Practise eating & drinking as on race day.

hmPace.title: Half marathon pace {n}×3 km
hmPace.desc: Race-pace specific: {warm} easy warm-up, then {n}×3 km at your target half-marathon pace with 2 min easy jogging after each. {cool} cool-down. The pace should feel controlled – the way you want to hold it for 21 km on race day.

vo2.desc800: {warm} warm-up. Then {n}×800 m hard (Z5 – only single words possible) at your target pace, with ~2:30 min very easy jogging in between. {cool} cool-down. Keep all intervals at the same speed – better even than a first one that’s too fast.
vo2.title: VO₂max {n}×{m} m
vo2.desc400: {warm} warm-up. Then {n}×400 m fast (Z5) around your 5 km race pace, with ~90 s very easy jogging in between. {cool} cool-down. Short, sharp, clean – the speed for your 5 km race.
vo2.desc1000: {warm} warm-up. {n}×1000 m hard (Z5) at 5–10 km pace, with ~2:30 min easy jogging in between. {cool} cool-down. Stay even all the way.

pyramid.title: VO₂max pyramid {seq} min
pyramid.desc: {warm} warm-up. Then a pyramid: {seq} min hard (Z5) with 90 s very easy jogging after each. The {peak}-minute step in the middle is the high point – hold it evenly, don’t overdo it. {cool} cool-down.

pace10k.title: 10 km race pace {n}×1000 m
pace10k.desc: {warm} warm-up. Then {n}×1000 m at your target 10 km race pace with ~2:30 min jog recovery after each. {cool} cool-down. This is how race pace feels – controlled, not flat out.

taper.raceDesc: {warm} warm-up, {n}×2 km at race pace with 3 min jog recovery, {cool} cool-down. Remind your legs of the pace – the volume is deliberately small, your freshness now comes from recovery.
taper.tempoDesc: {warm} warm-up, {n}×{min} min at threshold (Z4) with a long 3 min break, {cool} cool-down. Keep the stimulus, cut the volume – your sharpness now comes from recovery.

runWalk.title: Run-walk {n}×{min} min
runWalk.desc: Walk briskly for 5 min, then {n}× alternate {min} min of easy running with 1 min of walking, and finish with 5 min of walking. Run at a pace where you can still chat – the walk breaks are part of the plan, not giving up.

walk.title: Brisk walk
walk.desc: 30 min brisk walking – active recovery that keeps your circulation going without loading your legs. Counts fully as exercise.

long.easyDesc: Calm and steady in Z2 – base endurance for the eight running kilometres between the stations. Pace doesn’t matter.
long.title: Long run {km}
long.bikeAlt: Bike alternative (also easy on your back): ~{from}–{to} km or 1.5–2.5 h easy in Z2 instead of the run.
long.bikeAltRaceBlock: Bike alternative (also easy on your back): ~{from}–{to} km or 1.5–2.5 h easy in Z2 – but then no extra bike ride today.
long.leadTaper: Taper – shorter than recently, build up freshness.
long.raceBlockDesc: {km} in total: start easy in Z2, run {block} at race pace{pace} in one go in the middle, then ease back into an easy finish. Practise eating & drinking as on race day.
long.finish: Run the last 2 km briskly at marathon pace – a small stimulus that teaches tired legs to hold the pace.
long.desc: Calm long run, steady in Z2 throughout – fat metabolism & base endurance. Take a few sips every 20 min.

swim.techDesc: {m} m warm-up, 6×50 m technique drills (e.g. catch-up, fist swimming), then {reps}×100 m brisk with 20 s rest, {m} m easy cool-down. Calm, long strokes and clean breathing – technique over rush.
swim.raceDesc: Swim the race distance ({m} m) once in one go at your planned race pace – ideally in open water (in a wetsuit if it’s allowed in the race). Warm up easily before, 200 m easy afterwards.
swim.enduranceDesc: Steady swimming: 3×{m} m with 30 s rest at a calm base pace. Practise sighting along the way (look ahead every 6–8 strokes).

bike.baseDesc: Steady in Z2, cadence ~85–95 – pedal in smooth circles, don’t stomp.
bike.buildDesc: After 15 min warm-up, 4×5 min at threshold (Z4) with 3 min easy spinning in between. Then cool down.
bike.peakDesc: After 15 min warm-up, 3×10 min at your planned race pace (Z3–Z4) with 3 min easy spinning in between. Then cool down.
bike.taperDesc: Easy in Z2 with 4×30 s brisk efforts along the way. Stay fresh.
bike.title: Bike training
bike.longDesc: Long, calm ride in Z2 (~{dur} min), eat & drink well.
bike.brick: Straight afterwards, run easy for 10–15 min (brick training) – so your legs get used to switching from bike to run.

hyrox.baseDesc: {rounds} rounds, four stations each at half race volume: SkiErg 500 m · Wall Balls 30× · Sandbag Lunges 40 m · Rowing 500 m. No running in between – technique before speed, 90 s rest per round. No sled? Weighted squats or a wall sit instead.
hyrox.buildDesc: {rounds} rounds: run 1 km briskly, then straight into a station – alternating SkiErg 1000 m, Sled Push 50 m (or squats 20×), Burpee Broad Jumps 40 m, Rowing 1000 m, Farmer’s carry 200 m, Wall Balls 50×. This teaches your legs to find your running pace again after a station.
hyrox.simDesc: {rounds}× (1 km at your planned race pace + one station in race order: SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jumps, Rowing, Farmer’s carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls). Like on race day: start controlled, move quickly through the Roxzone, test your fuelling. Then two easy days.
hyrox.peakDesc: {rounds} rounds: one station at full race volume at your planned pace, then run 500 m briskly. 2 min rest between rounds. Start with your weakest stations.
hyrox.taperDesc: 4× (500 m brisk + half a station), 2 min rest. Stay fresh and let the routines settle.

near.shakeoutDesc: Very easy with a few strides. Wake your legs up before the race.
near.bikeCheckDesc: Spin easily, check gears and brakes, three short surges.
near.activationDesc: {warm} easy, 3×{min} min at race pace with 2 min jog recovery, 4 strides. Sharp but short.
near.easyShortDesc: Easy – stay fresh for the race.
near.lastLongerDesc: Calm in Z2 – your last slightly longer run before the race, no pace work.
near.swimDesc: Easy warm-up, 4×50 m at race pace, easy cool-down. Keep your feel for the water.
near.rideDesc: Easy in Z2 with 3×1 min at race pace in between.
near.brickDesc: 35 min easy on the bike, then straight into 10 min of easy running – keeps the transition familiar without tiring you.
near.hyroxDesc: One short technique round per station at half volume, no running at the limit. Go through the transitions and the order once more.

steadyRun.title: Steady easy run
steadyRun.desc: Steady in the base zone (Z2), conversational pace – you should be able to chat as you go. Rather a bit too slow than too fast; volume counts here, not pace.
steadyRun.backAlt: With back pain, do a steady bike ride (Z2) instead.

football.title: Football
football.desc: Team training – counts as cross-training (accelerations, speed, joy of the game). Warm up well, then jog easily for 5–10 min afterwards. If it was intense, take your next run a bit easier.

mobility.title: Mobility & stretching
mobility.desc: Calm mobility, 10–15 min, especially kind to your back: Cat-cow 10× · Hip flexor stretch 45 s/side · Gentle hamstring stretch 45 s/side · Calf stretch against the wall 45 s/side · Chest opener & supine twist 8×/side · Child’s pose 60 s. Nothing jerky – breathe gently into each position.

recovery.title: Recovery run
recovery.desc: Very easy in Z1–Z2, noticeably slower than your steady runs – if it feels “almost too easy”, it’s just right. Your legs should recover; pace doesn’t matter. Alternatively, an easy bike ride that’s gentle on your back.

extra.title: Easy run
extra.desc: Short and easy in Z2 – build volume without getting tired. No pace, no ambition.

tactic.5k: Start controlled (don’t overdo it!), pick it up from halfway and give everything in the last third.
tactic.10k: Even at race pace, pick it up bit by bit from km 7.
tactic.hm: Start evenly, give everything from km {km}.
tactic.marathon: Start deliberately conservatively and stay even – the race is decided from km {km}. Fuel as in training.

race.triDesc: Race day! {format}: {swim} m swim · {bike} km bike · {run} km run.{target} Swim: settle calmly into your rhythm, don’t burn out in the pack. Bike: steady, don’t overpace – you’ll still need your legs; drink regularly. Transitions quick but without rushing. Run: take the first 1–2 km deliberately easy, then build.
race.hyroxSplits: Guide values for {time}: about {run} min per running kilometre and about {station} min per station including the Roxzone.
race.hyroxDesc: Race day! 8 × 1 km running, with a station after each kilometre: SkiErg 1000 m · Sled Push 50 m · Sled Pull 50 m · Burpee Broad Jumps 80 m · Rowing 1000 m · Farmer’s carry 200 m · Sandbag Lunges 100 m · Wall Balls 100 reps (weights depending on your division).{target}{splits} Run the first kilometres deliberately controlled – the stations cost more than you think. Move quickly through the Roxzone but breathe calmly; do the wall balls in fixed sets with short breaks.

strides.title: Easy with strides
strides.raceWeekDesc: The activation run would sit right next to a hard fixed appointment – that appointment already wakes your legs up. So just easy in Z2 with 4 strides of ~20 s at the end. Stay fresh for the race.
strides.desc: This week your quality session would sit right next to a hard fixed appointment – the appointment provides the intensity. So an easy run in Z2 with 4–6 strides of ~20 s at the end (brisk, no sprinting; jog easily in between). That keeps your speed without two hard days in a row.

consolidate.name: Consolidate
consolidate.focus: Harder variations, lock in the habit

fitness.label: General fitness
fitness.desc: Endurance, strength and mobility following the WHO activity guidelines: endurance rises from about 120 to 150–180 minutes a week (brisk walking counts), plus strength on two days.

strength.label: Strength & muscle
strength.desc: Focus on strength training (alternating full-body sessions, two to three strength days) with some endurance and mobility for recovery. Strength progresses through rounds, reps and harder variations.

weightloss.label: Weight loss
weightloss.desc: Lots of movement (endurance and brisk walking, from about 150 to 225–240 minutes a week) plus strength on two days for your metabolism. Works best together with the calorie balance in Nutrition.

mobility.label: Mobility & health
mobility.desc: A gentle start: mobility, gentle strength on two days and activity that grows from about 90 to 150 minutes a week – ideal for beginners or for getting back into it.

fullBody.title: Strength – Full body
fullBody.moves: Squats 12× · Push-ups 8–12× (on your knees if needed) · Lunges 10×/leg · Shoulder press 12× · Plank 30–45 s
fullBody.harder: weighted squats, push-ups with feet raised, plank 60 s

lowerBody.title: Strength – Lower body
lowerBody.moves: Squats 15× · Romanian deadlift (dumbbell/kettlebell or single-leg) 10× · Step-ups onto a bench/step 10×/leg · Calf raises 20× · Glute bridge 15×
lowerBody.harder: Bulgarian split squats instead of step-ups, glute bridge on one leg, more weight

upperBody.title: Strength – Upper body & core
upperBody.moves: Push-ups 8–12× · Rows (dumbbell/band) 12× · Shoulder press 12× · Plank 40 s · Side plank 30 s/side · Dead bug 10×/side
upperBody.harder: close-grip push-ups, a stronger band or heavier dumbbell, side plank with leg raises

gentle.title: Gentle strength
gentle.moves: Sit-to-stand from a chair 10× · Wall push-ups 10× · Glute bridge 12× · Calf raises holding a chair 15× · On all fours, opposite arm and leg 8×/side
gentle.harder: lower more slowly, add short holds, only then more reps

strength.howIntro: Getting started: 2 rounds, technique before speed – better a few reps fewer, but clean.
strength.howBuild: 3 rounds. Every one to two weeks, add 1–2 reps or a little more weight, as long as your technique stays clean.

block.cardioDesc: Steady cardio at a conversational pace (Z2) – running, cycling, elliptical or swimming, whatever you like. You should be able to chat as you go. {total}
block.walkDesc: A brisk walk, ideally in the fresh air – fast enough that you breathe a little harder but can still talk. Easy to start and gentle on your joints, it counts fully as endurance. {total}
block.mobilityDesc: Calm mobility session: Cat-cow 10× · Hip flexor stretch 45 s/side · Gentle hamstring stretch 45 s/side · Chest opener & supine twist 8×/side · Child’s pose 60 s. Breathe gently into each position, nothing jerky.

healthImport.title: Health import
healthImport.autoIntro: Let your iPhone send your weight, heart rate, HRV, VO₂max, sleep and workouts automatically every day. Two ways: the “Health Auto Export” app (automatic transfer needs Premium – about €8 a year or €30 one-off according to the App Store) or, for free, a shortcut in Apple’s “Shortcuts” app (daily values without workouts). Both use the address below.
healthImport.androidText: A bridge app such as the open-source “HC Webhook” sends weight, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep, steps and workouts from Health Connect to the same address – with the same key.
healthImport.fullText: Alternatively, the complete history as a file: export it on your iPhone and upload it here – as often as you like. Duplicate entries are recognised automatically.
healthImport.step1: iPhone: open the Health app → tap your profile picture at the top.
healthImport.step2: Choose “Export All Health Data” – this creates a ZIP file.
healthImport.step3: Move the ZIP to your iPad or computer with AirDrop/Files, or upload it straight from here.

healthImport.ingestIntro: Weight, resting heart rate, HRV, VO₂max, sleep & workouts straight from Apple Health – daily and incrementally via the “Health Auto Export” app. No 300 MB upload. Switching it on creates a personal access token.
healthImport.keyNote: Key and URL belong together – don’t share them. Automations you’ve already set up with “&token=” in the URL keep working.
healthImport.newTokenText: The current key stops working – you’ll need to replace it in “Health Auto Export”.
healthImport.hcStep1: Install a bridge app on the Android device that sends Health Connect data as JSON via webhook – for example “HC Webhook” (open source).
healthImport.hcStep2: Tap “Switch on auto-import” at the top, then enter the endpoint URL as the webhook address.
healthImport.hcStep3: Send the key as the “X-Catofit-Token” header. If the app can’t set headers, append it to the address: …&token=<key>.
healthImport.hcStep4: In the app, allow these data types: weight, body fat, lean mass, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep, steps, active calories, workouts and heart rate (for the average heart rate of your workouts). Cycle data only if you want to bring it over – it stays private.
healthImport.hcStep5: Switch syncing on. Your values appear at the next sync; Cat-O-Fit recognises days and workouts that are sent twice.
healthImport.hcIntro: Health Connect can only be reached by apps on the device, not by websites. That’s why a small bridge app handles the transfer:
healthImport.hcNote: Daily values belong to the calendar day in your server’s time zone; HRV from Health Connect is RMSSD and is evaluated separately from Apple values (SDNN).
healthImport.aeIntro: That way your iPhone sends your key values to Cat-O-Fit every day – small and automatic. Set it up once:
healthImport.aeStep1: Install the “Health Auto Export – JSON+CSV” app from the App Store and open it. Automatic transfer needs Premium (about €8 a year or €30 one-off according to the App Store).
healthImport.aeStep2: At the bottom, tap “Automations” → “+” → choose “REST API” as the type.
healthImport.aeStep3: Under “URL”, paste the endpoint URL you copied; method “POST”, format “JSON” (export version 2).
healthImport.aeStep4: Under “Headers”, add: key “X-Catofit-Token”, value = the key you copied. (That way it never shows up in a server log.)
healthImport.aeStep5: Only if there is an extra sign-in in front of your site (reverse proxy with Basic Auth): also add “Authorization: Basic …” under “Headers”. Without such a sign-in – for example with the container’s built-in Basic Auth – you can skip this.
healthImport.aeStep6: Choose metrics: weight, body fat, lean mass (Lean Body Mass), resting heart rate, HRV, VO₂max, sleep, steps, active energy – plus “Workouts”.
healthImport.aeStep7: Aggregation “daily”, schedule “daily”, period “Since last sync” (sends new data only) – for big backfills, switch on “Batch requests”.
healthImport.aeStep8: Save → “Run now” to test. The values show up in Cat-O-Fit after the next sync.
healthImport.aeHistory: For the 10-year history, send larger periods once (e.g. one month at a time) – weight can go in completely, denser values for 1–2 years.
healthImport.aeShortcut: For free, use a shortcut (“Find Health Samples” → “Get Contents of URL”, JSON like { "date": "2026-09-29", "weight": "72.4" }) to the same address with the same header – step by step in the “Apple Health” docs.

eligibility.blockMinor: For children and teenagers Cat-O-Fit doesn’t work out calorie or weight targets. What matters is eating enough and eating a varied diet – especially on training days.

sportsMedicine.title: Sports medicine check-up
sportsMedicine.what: The route that really fits: a doctor with the additional qualification in sports medicine, often at sports-medicine institutes, university hospitals or larger practices. Usually a blood count, iron status, liver and kidney values – often together with performance testing.
sportsMedicine.tip: Many statutory health insurers subsidise the sports check-up as a voluntary extra benefit – roughly €60–200 depending on the insurer, usually every two years. Few people know this: just ask your insurer beforehand.

gp.title: GP or specialist practice
gp.what: Paid for by statutory insurance only with a medical reason – symptoms or a specific suspicion. “Ferritin, because I run a lot” is not a medical reason; it is then a self-pay service (IGeL) billed under the German fee schedule for doctors.
gp.cost: covered by insurance with a medical reason, otherwise about €20–60
gp.tip: If you have to give blood for something else anyway: ask whether the values you care about can be measured from the same sample.

checkup.title: Check-up 35 (statutory preventive care)
checkup.what: Once between 18 and 34, then every three years. Includes cholesterol, blood sugar and a urine test – but neither ferritin nor vitamin D.
checkup.tip: A good baseline check, but it covers only some of the values that matter for sport.

mailInLab.title: Mail-in and self-pay labs
mailInLab.what: Home test kits (capillary blood from a fingertip) or self-pay offers from conventional labs with a venous blood draw.
mailInLab.tip: Capillary blood is more sensitive to how it is taken than a venous blood draw. To compare values over time, stick to the same method and lab where you can.

bloodDonation.title: Blood donation
bloodDonation.what: Haemoglobin is measured at every donation; some donation services also measure ferritin in regular donors.
bloodDonation.tip: Donating regularly noticeably lowers your iron stores – if you do endurance sport, keeping an eye on your ferritin is especially worthwhile.

standards.rilibaek: The **RiliBÄK** (guideline of the German Medical Association) is binding for all German labs and regulates quality assurance, including external proficiency testing.
standards.isoAccreditation: Many labs are also accredited to **DIN EN ISO 15189**.
standards.dataExchange: For sending results to practices, **LDT** is the German standard and **HL7 FHIR** the international one. Through the **electronic patient record (ePA)**, results increasingly reach insured people digitally.
standards.referenceRanges: **Reference ranges are not uniform across Germany.** Every lab gives its own – depending on measurement method, device and reference population. For ferritin, fT3 or vitamin B12 they differ noticeably. That is why the range is always printed on the report: it belongs to the value.
standards.sportRanges: **There are no official sport-specific reference values.** What Cat-O-Fit shows as a sport target range comes from sports-medicine literature and international position statements – not from a German standard. The source for each value is in the detail view under “Basis of the ranges”.

labSources.teaser: You can get most values through a sports-medicine check-up (subsidised by many insurers), through your GP’s practice or through a mail-in lab.

ferritin.label: Ferritin
ferritin.source: Usual lab range; sport range after GSSI (Peeling, Sim, McKay); inflammation: WHO 2020; biological variation: Scand J Clin Lab Invest 2023
ferritin.hint: Iron stores. For endurance sport, values well above the lower lab limit are favourable – low stores can affect performance before anaemia shows up.

transferrinSat.label: Transferrin saturation
transferrinSat.source: GSSI (Peeling, Sim, McKay: below 16% stage 2 iron deficiency); EASL 2022 (above 45% with high ferritin: investigate)
transferrinSat.hint: How much iron is actually being transported – complements ferritin.

hb.label: Haemoglobin
hb.source: WHO 2024 (anaemia limits 12.0 g/dl women, 13.0 g/dl men, 11.0 g/dl in pregnancy); biological variation: EFLM 2019
hb.hint: Oxygen transport. With endurance sport often slightly low because of the larger blood plasma volume (“pseudo-anaemia”) – that is not a deficiency.

crp.label: CRP
crp.source: IQWiG, gesundheitsinformation.de (up to 5 mg/l or 0.5 mg/dl); raised after endurance exercise: Thomas, Labor und Diagnose, ch. 51
crp.hint: Inflammation marker. Briefly raised after hard sessions; persistently high values suggest your body is not coping well with the load.

vitaminD.label: Vitamin D (25-OH)
vitaminD.source: DGE 2012 (sufficient from 50 nmol/l); IOC 2018 and Endocrine Society 2024 (no consensus on higher targets)
vitaminD.hint: Contributes to the normal function of muscles, bones and the immune system. At our latitudes the level regularly drops from October to March. Some sports doctors aim for 75 nmol/l – there is no consensus on that, so the DGE value applies here.

b12.label: Vitamin B12 (holo-TC)
b12.source: LADR laboratory group (below 35 deficiency likely, 35–50 grey area, above 50 unlikely; no upper limit)
b12.hint: Holotranscobalamin shows the actively available form – more informative than total B12. Particularly relevant on a vegetarian or vegan diet.

b12total.label: Vitamin B12 (total)
b12total.source: Usual lab classification (below 150 pmol/l or 200 pg/ml deficiency likely; in the grey area holo-TC or methylmalonic acid)
b12total.hint: Total B12, which is measured more often, is less informative than holo-TC. Don’t mix them up: the numbers are much higher than for holo-TC.
b12total.grey: grey area – have holo-TC or MMA measured

folate.label: Folate
folate.source: Usual lab range (depends on the lab – enter your own range)
folate.hint: Important for blood formation and cell division.

magnesium.label: Magnesium (whole blood)
magnesium.source: Whole-blood lab ranges: Medizinische Laboratorien Düsseldorf 1.28–1.69; Medics Labor 1.28–1.83; Labor Mustafa 1.2–1.72 mmol/l (method-dependent)
magnesium.hint: Measured in whole blood (heparin or EDTA tube). The ranges depend heavily on the method – enter your lab’s range. The more commonly measured serum value goes under “Magnesium (serum)”.

magnesiumSerum.label: Magnesium (serum)
magnesiumSerum.source: Usual serum range (e.g. 0.70–1.10 mmol/l, Medizinische Laboratorien Düsseldorf)
magnesiumSerum.hint: Serum magnesium is the most common lab value for magnesium. It reflects the stores only roughly.

zinc.label: Zinc
zinc.hint: Immune function and recovery; losses through sweat matter at high training volume.

selenium.label: Selenium
selenium.hint: Antioxidant protection and thyroid metabolism. Overdosing is harmful – don’t exceed the target range.

sodium.label: Sodium
sodium.hint: During very long efforts with a lot of drinking, sodium can drop dangerously (hyponatraemia).

tsh.label: TSH
tsh.source: Usual lab range; biotin interference: BfR

ft3.label: fT3
ft3.source: Usual lab range; low fT3 as a sign of low energy availability: IOC 2023 (REDs)
ft3.hint: Often drops early when energy is low for a long time – a warning sign of too little energy relative to training.

testosterone.label: Testosterone (total)
testosterone.source: Usual lab ranges by sex; low values as a sign of low energy availability: IOC 2023 (REDs)
testosterone.hint: Falls with a lasting energy deficit and overtraining.

estradiol.label: Oestradiol
estradiol.source: Usual lab range for men; for women by cycle phase according to your own lab (IOC 2023: cycle status cannot be assessed under hormonal contraception)
estradiol.hint: Varies strongly with the cycle – for women it can only be assessed together with the cycle day and your lab’s range for that phase. Persistently low values plus a missing period are a warning sign.

ck.label: Creatine kinase (CK)
ck.source: Usual lab ranges by sex; female athletes 47–513 and male athletes 82–1083 U/l: Thomas, Labor und Diagnose, ch. 51
ck.hint: Marker of muscle strain. Strongly raised after hard sessions – only meaningful after at least one rest day.

urea.label: Urea
urea.source: Usual lab range; raised up to 24 h after a marathon: Thomas, Labor und Diagnose, ch. 51
urea.hint: Rises with a high training load and a high-protein diet; persistently high values suggest incomplete recovery.

labs.sourceLabDependent: Usual lab range (depends on the lab)
labs.blockedNeedsSex: The ranges for {label} differ by sex. Enter your sex in your profile, or your lab’s range with the value.
labs.blockedCycle: {label} varies a lot across the cycle.{day} The value can only be assessed using the range your lab gives for this phase of the cycle – enter it with the value.
labs.blockedExercise: You trained hard before the blood draw – {label} is often temporarily raised then. Have it measured again at rest (after at least one day without training).
labs.caveatCrp: CRP from the same blood draw: {crp} mg/l. Ferritin rises with inflammation – a value below 70 µg/l then still points to iron deficiency (WHO 2020).
labs.blockedCrp: CRP from the same blood draw is {crp} mg/l – {label} rises with inflammation and can’t be meaningfully assessed then. Measure again once it has settled.
labs.errorBothLimits: {label}: please enter both limits of the reference range – or neither
labs.errorUpperLimit: {label}: the upper limit must be greater than the lower one
labs.blockedNoRange: There is no range stored for this value.
labs.caveatBiotin: Biotin (also in skin, hair and combination supplements) can distort this test – after checking with your doctor, pause it for a few days before your next blood draw.
labs.inflamedLow: low despite inflammation – points to iron deficiency
labs.caveatNoCrp: Without a CRP from the same blood draw, the assessment comes with a reservation – ferritin rises with inflammation.
labs.highForAthletes: above the lab range, common in people who train – recheck at rest
labs.normalButTight: within the normal range, but on the low side for sport
labs.normalButHigh: within the normal range, but high

vitaminD.label: Vitamin D
vitaminD.food: Oily fish (salmon, herring), egg yolk, mushrooms – and in summer 15 minutes of sun on your arms and face.
vitaminD.timing: With a meal that contains fat (it is fat-soluble).
vitaminD.ul: EFSA upper limit: 4,000 IU (100 µg) per day – above that only under medical supervision.
vitaminD.note: If you have a known deficiency, recheck your level after 3 months.

magnesium.label: Magnesium
magnesium.typical: up to 250 mg per day from supplements, split into two portions
magnesium.food: Oats, nuts, pulses, wholegrain, dark chocolate, magnesium-rich mineral water.
magnesium.timing: Often taken in the evening – spaced apart from iron and zinc.
magnesium.ul: More than 250 mg per day from supplements often causes loose stools (EFSA upper limit).
magnesium.note: Citrate or glycinate are better tolerated than oxide.

iron.label: Iron
iron.typical: only after talking to a doctor
iron.food: Red meat, pulses, oats, millet – eaten together with vitamin C (peppers, citrus).
iron.timing: On an empty stomach or with vitamin C; at least 2 hours apart from coffee, tea, milk and calcium.
iron.ul: Never take it without a lab value – with full stores, iron is harmful.
iron.note: Any iron supplementation should be supervised and monitored by a doctor.

b12.label: Vitamin B12
b12.typical: up to 25 µg per day as a supplement; on a purely plant-based diet, higher amounts are usual after talking to a doctor
b12.food: Meat, fish, eggs, dairy. A purely plant-based diet doesn’t meet the need – here a supplement is the norm.
b12.ul: No upper limit set; higher amounts only with a reason.

creatine.label: Creatine (monohydrate)
creatine.food: Red meat and fish – the effective amount is hardly reachable through food.
creatine.timing: Every day at the same time; the time of day doesn’t matter. The effect builds up over about 3–4 weeks.
creatine.ul: Well studied; with healthy kidneys the usual amount is considered safe. Drink enough.
creatine.note: At first 1–2 kg more on the scales from water in the muscle – that isn’t fat.

protein.label: Protein powder
protein.typical: only to top up your daily amount
protein.food: Quark, skyr, cottage cheese, eggs, fish, pulses – powder is pure convenience, not a magic potion.
protein.timing: Spread across the day; 20–40 g per portion is usual.
protein.ul: No limit set; prefer protein from real food.
protein.source: ACSM 2016 (1.2–2.0 g per kg body weight)

caffeine.label: Caffeine
caffeine.typical: about 3 mg per kg body weight; if you have no experience with it, no more than 200 mg at once
caffeine.timing: 45–60 minutes before the effort. Take the last dose at least 8 hours before bedtime.
caffeine.ul: More than 400 mg per day (adults) increases restlessness, palpitations and sleep problems.
caffeine.note: Try it in training first – never for the first time in a race.

beetroot.label: Beetroot concentrate (nitrate)
beetroot.timing: 2–3 hours before the effort; try it in the days before.
beetroot.ul: No need to take it continuously – used as needed before races.
beetroot.note: Studied mainly for efforts lasting 5–30 minutes.

betaAlanine.label: Beta-alanine
betaAlanine.timing: Split into several small portions – that reduces the tingling on the skin.
betaAlanine.ul: Larger single portions cause skin tingling – so split them.
betaAlanine.note: Studied mainly for hard efforts of 30 seconds to 10 minutes.

electrolytes.label: Electrolytes (sodium)
electrolytes.typical: 300–700 mg sodium per hour during long efforts
electrolytes.timing: During long sessions over 90 minutes, especially in the heat.
electrolytes.ul: Only with matching effort – not as a permanent addition.
electrolytes.note: In very long efforts, sodium protects against dangerously low blood levels.

omega3.label: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)
omega3.food: Salmon, herring, mackerel twice a week; plant-based: linseed oil and walnuts.
omega3.ul: More than 3,000 mg per day only after talking to a doctor (blood clotting); EFSA considers up to 5 g safe.

zinc.label: Zinc
zinc.typical: up to 6.5 mg per day from supplements
zinc.food: Meat, cheese, oats, pumpkin seeds, lentils.
zinc.timing: Not at the same time as iron or calcium.
zinc.ul: Permanently more than 25 mg per day interferes with copper absorption (EFSA upper limit).

interaction.ironZinc: Iron and zinc compete for the same absorption routes – take them several hours apart.
interaction.ironMagnesium: Magnesium (and calcium) slow iron absorption – iron in the morning, magnesium in the evening.
interaction.caffeineIron: Coffee and tea clearly inhibit iron absorption – keep at least two hours apart.
interaction.zincMagnesium: Take zinc and magnesium at different times, otherwise they get in each other’s way.

supplements.ironInflamedReason: Ferritin {value} µg/l ({date}) – {assessment}. The CRP from the same blood draw is raised.
supplements.ferritinFalling: Over several measurements, ferritin has been falling by more than the usual variation (about {rate} µg/l per month) and, at this pace, will reach the tight range {when}.
supplements.vitaminDOld: Your last vitamin D value ({date}) is from a different season or is more than four months old.
supplements.proteinReason: According to your food diary you average {value} g of protein per kg body weight ({days} days) – 1.2–2.0 g per kg is usual for training.

creatineReason.one: {count} strength session in the last four weeks – for building strength and muscle, creatine is the best-studied supplement.
creatineReason.other: {count} strength sessions in the last four weeks – for building strength and muscle, creatine is the best-studied supplement.

supplements.dopingNote: For races with doping controls, only use batch-tested products (e.g. from the Cologne List) – supplements are contaminated more often than you would think.
supplements.tooHighAction: Don’t supplement (any further). If you take a supplement, review your intake and have the value assessed by a doctor.
supplements.ironInflamedWait: Have ferritin measured again once the inflammation has settled – no iron before then.
supplements.ironInflamedAction: Get it checked by a doctor: with inflammation, iron is absorbed poorly – whether and when iron makes sense is for the doctor to decide.
supplements.ironLowAction: Get it checked by a doctor: only with a lab report can you decide whether – and how much – iron makes sense. Until then, boost your iron through food.
supplements.ironHighAction: Don’t take iron. Have high stores assessed by a doctor (e.g. with the transferrin saturation).
supplements.ironFallingAction: No supplement needed yet – eat more iron-rich food and have it measured again in about three months.
supplements.vitaminDDeficientAction: A deficiency should be managed by a doctor – agree the amount and follow-up checks with them.
supplements.vitaminDLowAction: Supplementing through the dark months is usual in this case – have your level rechecked after about three months.
supplements.vitaminDWinter: Between October and March, the sun at our latitudes isn’t strong enough for your body to make vitamin D itself.
supplements.vitaminDMeasureAction: Have your level measured once – it’s the most reliable basis. Without a value, the DGE recommends 20 µg (800 IU) a day when there is no sun.
supplements.b12LowAction: Supplementing is usual in this case – have your level rechecked after about three months.
supplements.b12GreyAction: In the grey area, measuring methylmalonic acid or homocysteine shows whether there is really a deficiency.
supplements.b12TotalAction: Total B12 is not very specific: have holo-TC or methylmalonic acid measured and the result assessed by a doctor.
supplements.veganReason: A purely plant-based diet doesn’t cover your B12 needs.
supplements.veganAction: Here a supplement isn’t an extra but a necessity – long term, with an occasional check of your level.
supplements.magnesiumAction: Eat magnesium-rich foods first; a supplement is possible (often taken in the evening).
supplements.proteinAction: Cover it with real food first; use powder only if you can’t reach your daily amount otherwise.
supplements.creatineAction: Only worthwhile if you need it and train strength long term; the usual amount is listed below.
supplements.cycleIronReason: People who menstruate and do endurance sport regularly lose iron – but without a lab value the stores can’t be judged.
supplements.cycleIronAction: Have ferritin (together with CRP) measured before considering an iron supplement.
supplements.foodFirst: Food first, then the supplement: what ends up on your plate works more reliably than any capsule – and it’s cheaper.
supplements.ironBorderline: within the normal range, but tight for endurance sport

labsView.introWhat: Log values from your lab report, see their trend and get a sport-specific assessment – for example, that a ferritin of 25 is “normal” but on the low side for endurance training.
labsView.introGate: First, a quick boundary: Cat-O-Fit is meant for healthy adults. If you are under medical treatment, take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have an eating disorder, use this module only for documenting – the app deliberately gives no recommendations then. Your answers apply to the whole app.
